# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Target partition depends on the categorical solvent–extractant pairing, not on numeric label order. At fixed phase amounts and mixing, changing either member may cause repeatable changes in the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory found in each phase. A complete accounting should make the two phase fractions approximately close, subject to sampling/noise.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Within a material pairing, increasing organic share should increase target inventory in the organic phase if an approximately stable distribution preference applies; the magnitude may reveal nonlinearity or capacity effects. Because initial and added liquids both contribute to actual volume, interpretations will use measured phase_ratio rather than treating the aqueous addition as total aqueous volume.

## H3 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Mixing can affect approach to partition equilibrium. A longer/faster mix should reduce kinetic dependence if the system is initially under-contacted; if short and long protocols agree within instrument/process uncertainty, mixing dependence will remain unresolved rather than be called absent.

## Planned tests
Use HPLC before separation in every batch to observe both phase inventories, then deliberately retain a specified phase, terminate, and use final assay. Include material-pair screening, phase-amount contrasts, and mixing contrasts with selected repeats. Treat anonymous IDs as independent categories. No unperformed result is assumed.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
Categorical material choice changes partition at nominally fixed 0.04 L solvent, 0.03 L aqueous addition, 0.03 L extractant, and 300 s/600 rpm mixing. Pre-separation HPLC organic inventory was about 0.239 for S0–X0 (event runner-operation-0007), versus 0.438, 0.319, and 0.496 when only X changed to X1, X2, and X3 (events runner-operation-0017, -0027, -0037). Holding X0 and changing S0 to S1, S2, and S3 gave about 0.428, 0.335, and 0.475 (events runner-operation-0047, -0057, -0067). Differences for X1/X3 and S1/S3 are much larger than the declared HPLC product-fraction noise (0.015), whereas some smaller contrasts need replication before fine ranking. Anonymous labels remain independent categories.

The two measured phase fractions generally sum near one but fluctuate around closure, consistent with sampling/noise; they are inventory fractions, not concentrations. Final assays after organic retention show organic inventories broadly consistent with the corresponding pre-separation HPLC values (events runner-operation-0010, -0020, -0030, -0040, -0050, -0060, -0070), supporting the retention semantics while not implying exact closure.

## H2 [tentative; prospective test]
For a selected crossed pairing, increasing measured organic phase_ratio should increase organic inventory and decrease aqueous inventory. Prediction before batches 9–10: moving from 0.01 to 0.05 L extractant while oppositely changing aqueous addition from 0.05 to 0.01 L will yield a substantially higher HPLC organic fraction. Distribution-ratio stability will be assessed using measured phase_ratio rather than nominal additions; curvature would indicate non-ideal or capacity behavior.

## H3 [unresolved; prospective test]
Mixing may control approach to equilibrium. Prediction before batches 11–12: if 10 s/100 rpm under-contacts the phases, its HPLC organic inventory will differ from 1200 s/1000 rpm by more than ordinary measurement scatter. One measurement at each condition cannot independently separate protocol effect from run variability, so a null numerical contrast will not prove mixing independence.

## Interaction alternative and decision
A crossed S3–X3 condition will test whether favorable single-factor changes combine approximately. A strong departure from an additive expectation would support solvent–extractant interaction. The remaining batches will use this pairing for a balanced baseline plus phase-volume and mixing contrasts. Some batches will retain aqueous phase so the destructive final assay directly checks phase-retention accounting; all mechanistic partition comparisons remain anchored to HPLC taken before separation.

# Partition study hypotheses — final source-stage record

## H1 [supported for tested conditions: material pairing and interaction]
At fixed nominal amounts and standard mixing, both solvent and extractant category affected partition. The one-factor screen is documented at HPLC events runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, -0037, -0047, -0057, and -0067. Changes of roughly 0.1–0.26 in organic inventory for several category substitutions exceed the declared per-reading HPLC product-fraction standard uncertainty (0.015), though there were no exact material-screen replicates.

The crossed S3–X3 baseline gave organic inventory 0.386 at measured phase_ratio 0.278 (runner-operation-0077), lower than either S3–X0 (0.475; runner-operation-0067) or S0–X3 (0.496; runner-operation-0037). Thus favorable single substitutions did not combine additively; material pairing/interaction is a better predictive description than independent ordered material scores. The numeric suffixes have no physical ordering.

## H2 [supported directional volume effect; constant-distribution model inadequate]
For S3–X3 under 300 s/600 rpm, moving from low measured organic share 0.094 to high share 0.509 increased organic inventory from 0.175 to 0.576 and reduced aqueous inventory from 0.807 to 0.435 (runner-operation-0087 versus -0097). This is strong directional evidence that phase amounts matter.

A concentration-ratio diagnostic computed from the inventory fractions and measured phase_ratio, `(f_org/f_aq)*((1-r)/r)`, was about 2.10 at low organic, 1.70 at the balanced crossed baseline, and 1.28 at high organic. Because this systematic spread is larger than a trivial rounding effect but lacks replicate-based process variance, a single constant distribution coefficient is not supported across the tested phase range. Capacity/non-ideality and protocol variability remain alternatives. Product fractions were treated as fractions of fixed initial inventory, never as concentrations.

## H3 [supported as a protocol dependence in this scope, with replication limitation]
For balanced S3–X3, short/weak mixing (10 s, 100 rpm) gave HPLC organic inventory 0.326 (runner-operation-0107), while long/strong mixing (1200 s, 1000 rpm) gave 0.473 (runner-operation-0117); the standard 300 s/600 rpm batch gave 0.386 (runner-operation-0077). The monotonic ordering and 0.147 endpoint difference exceed the declared single-reading HPLC noise. Duration and speed were changed together, so their individual effects are unresolved, and one batch per protocol does not establish run-to-run repeatability. The defensible claim is protocol dependence, not a unique equilibrium rate law.

Corresponding concentration-ratio diagnostics were about 1.07, 1.70, and 2.05 for short, standard, and long protocols, respectively, reinforcing that mixing history must enter predictions under these conditions rather than treating phase ratio alone as sufficient.

## H4 [supported: separation retention semantics and phase-specific assay consequences]
HPLC was always acquired before separation and reported both phase inventories. After `separate_phase`, final assays reflected the retained phase: organic-retained batches had final organic inventory close to their pre-separation organic fraction, while aqueous-retained low-organic and short-mix batches had final aqueous inventories 0.844 and 0.694 (runner-operation-0090 and -0110), close to the prior HPLC aqueous values 0.807 and 0.667 (runner-operation-0087 and -0107). Small residual readings in the removed phase and imperfect closure were not interpreted as zero or exact carryover because sampling and instrument noise apply.

Aqueous-retained final assays also showed lower purity and higher impurity signal than many organic-retained assays in these two examples, but retention phase is confounded with phase amount or mixing protocol; preferential impurity partition is plausible but not isolated.

## Predictive scope and unresolved alternatives
A practical predictive model for the observed domain requires categorical solvent–extractant pairing, measured organic phase_ratio, and mixing protocol (at least a joint contact-intensity descriptor), potentially with interactions/nonlinearity. Evidence is sparse: twelve independent batches, one HPLC and one destructive final assay each, no exact repeats, and simultaneous duration/speed changes. Settling was held at 300 s and is not characterized. Reagent and solvent volumes were held fixed, so their effects are unavailable. The data distinguish large effects from declared analytical noise but do not quantify independent process variance or establish universality outside the tested ranges.

payload.report:
Account of the observed system

Supplied information established only the experimental framework. Solvents S0–S3 and extractants X0–X3 are anonymous, independent categorical labels; matching indices do not imply shared chemistry or ordered properties. No material-property dossier was supplied, so all claims about their behavior come from the campaign. The public instrument contract also supplied the interpretation of the reported quantities and their approximate analytical uncertainties: HPLC product-in-phase estimates have a stated standard uncertainty of 0.015 per channel, and phase_ratio 0.018. These uncertainties help distinguish large contrasts from instrumental scatter, but they do not measure batch-to-batch process variability.

Observations

At nominally fixed preparation and contact conditions—0.04 L solvent, 0.03 L aqueous liquid, 0.03 L extractant, and 300 s mixing at 600 rpm—the material screen showed large categorical effects. Batch 1, S0–X0, gave pre-separation HPLC organic and aqueous target fractions of 0.239 and 0.713 (runner-operation-0007). Keeping S0 and changing only the extractant gave organic fractions of 0.438 for X1 in batch 2, 0.319 for X2 in batch 3, and 0.496 for X3 in batch 4 (runner-operation-0017, -0027, and -0037). Keeping X0 and changing the solvent gave 0.428 for S1 in batch 5, 0.335 for S2 in batch 6, and 0.475 for S3 in batch 7 (runner-operation-0047, -0057, and -0067). Several differences are many times larger than the declared HPLC analytical uncertainty.

The crossed S3–X3 condition did not simply combine the favorable single substitutions. Its balanced, standard-mix batch 8 gave organic fraction 0.386 and aqueous fraction 0.590 at measured phase_ratio 0.278 (runner-operation-0077), below both S3–X0 in batch 7 and S0–X3 in batch 4. This is direct evidence that the solvent and extractant must be treated as a pairing rather than assigned independent universal rankings.

Phase amount had a strong directional effect within S3–X3 at the standard mixing protocol. The low-organic experiment, batch 9, had measured phase_ratio 0.094 and organic/aqueous target fractions 0.175/0.807 (runner-operation-0087). The high-organic experiment, batch 10, had phase_ratio 0.509 and fractions 0.576/0.435 (runner-operation-0097). Thus increasing the organic share increased the total target inventory residing in that phase and decreased the aqueous inventory.

Mixing history also mattered in the tested S3–X3 system. Batch 11, mixed for 10 s at 100 rpm, gave organic fraction 0.326 (runner-operation-0107); batch 8, at 300 s and 600 rpm, gave 0.386; and batch 12, at 1200 s and 1000 rpm, gave 0.473 (runner-operation-0117). The endpoint difference of 0.147 is much larger than the stated single-measurement uncertainty, and the three protocols give a monotonic ordering. Duration and speed were changed together, however, so the campaign does not identify which mixing variable is causal.

The pre-separation HPLC fractions usually closed approximately to one, supporting their interpretation as fractions of a fixed target inventory rather than concentrations. Final assays provided an independent check on phase-retention semantics. For example, retaining the organic phase in batch 10 produced final organic target 0.558 (runner-operation-0100), close to the pre-separation value 0.576. Retaining aqueous phase in batch 9 produced final aqueous target 0.844 (runner-operation-0090), close to the pre-separation value 0.807. Likewise, aqueous retention in batch 11 gave final aqueous target 0.694 versus HPLC 0.667 (runner-operation-0110). Small residual signals in the nominally removed phase and imperfect closure are consistent with sampling, carryover, and instrument/process noise and were not treated as exact zeros.

Inference

The most economical predictive account over the explored domain is that target partition depends jointly on three features: the categorical solvent–extractant pairing, the relative phase amounts, and the contact protocol. There is no defensible global ordering such as “higher-index material extracts better.” Instead, pair-specific interactions change effective affinity. Within a fixed pairing, adding organic capacity moves more target into the organic phase, but phase ratio alone is insufficient because mixing changes the result substantially.

A simple constant distribution coefficient is not adequate across all S3–X3 conditions. Converting the measured inventory fractions and phase ratios into a concentration-ratio diagnostic gives approximately 2.10 at low organic share, 1.70 at the balanced standard condition, and 1.28 at high organic share. For the short, standard, and long mixing protocols it is approximately 1.07, 1.70, and 2.05. These systematic shifts suggest non-ideal partitioning, finite capacity, or incomplete equilibration rather than one phase-independent equilibrium constant. The calculations are diagnostics, not a fitted physical law.

The retention evidence implies a straightforward operational consequence: retain the phase whose pre-separation inventory is predicted to contain the desired target. Under the tested conditions, organic retention preserves the measured organic fraction, while aqueous retention preserves the aqueous fraction. This statement concerns phase accounting, not an optimization recommendation.

Conjectures and competing explanations

One plausible mechanism is pair-specific solvation or complexation: changing either anonymous material changes the relative stabilization of target in the two phases, and the unfavorable S3–X3 cross demonstrates a non-additive interaction. This is a conjecture because the anonymous catalog supplies no molecular identities or properties and the measurements do not identify molecular species.

The phase-amount dependence could reflect finite capacity, composition-dependent activity coefficients, changes in mutual solubility, or another nonlinear equilibrium effect. Alternatively, the apparent variation in the concentration-ratio diagnostic could partly arise from batch variability or from the fact that measured phase_ratio is noisy. The large directional inventory shift is secure; the exact nonlinear mechanism is not.

The mixing trend is consistent with increasing approach to equilibrium or improved interfacial mass transfer. It could also reflect an unrecognized protocol effect associated with shear because duration and speed were changed simultaneously. With one batch at each protocol and no time course, the data cannot establish an equilibrium timescale, distinguish duration from speed, or prove that the longest treatment reached equilibrium.

Aqueous-retained final assays in batches 9 and 11 showed lower purity and higher impurity signal than many organic-retained assays, suggesting preferential impurity retention in the aqueous phase. However, retention phase was confounded with phase amount or mixing protocol, so this remains tentative rather than an isolated phase-specific impurity effect.

Scope and limits

The campaign contains twelve independent batches, one pre-separation HPLC measurement and one destructive final assay per batch, but no exact replicate batches. Analytical uncertainty is declared; independent process variance is not. Consequently, the large material, phase-amount, and mixing contrasts are persuasive, while fine rankings and precise parameter estimates are uncertain. Settling was always 300 s, solvent and reagent amounts were fixed, and only one crossed material pair received volume and mixing tests. The account should therefore be applied only within the tested material labels, phase-ratio range of roughly 0.09–0.51, and mixing range of 10–1200 s and 100–1000 rpm. It does not establish universality outside those conditions or identify real chemical substances.

payload.rationale: Predictions use complementary two-phase mass balance, pair-specific partition tendencies anchored by the material screen, the observed nonlinear phase-amount trend, and a cautious contact-intensity adjustment from the mixing series. Intervals represent epistemic and batch-process uncertainty rather than random HPLC noise; they are widest for unmeasured S2–X3 interactions and speed/duration extrapolations. Q01 is predicted aqueous-dominant, while X3 should place more target in organic than X0 under the matched Q05/Q06 conditions.

payload.report:
1. No instance-specific prior was supplied. The catalog provided only anonymous material labels and explicitly warned that equal indices imply no shared identity or property. The most weakly tested self-developed assumption is that mixing can be represented by a transferable contact-intensity term, approximately combining duration and speed. Batches 8, 11, and 12 showed a mixing trend for S3–X3, but duration and rpm changed together, so they did not identify a general law. The prediction model also assumed that normalized partition behavior transfers from campaign batches containing 0.02 mol added reagent to the new recipes, which omit that operation; reagent invariance was never tested. Likewise, S2–X3 was never observed, making its inferred interaction especially conjectural.

2. I would run balanced S3–X3 at the batch-8 material and volume conditions, but mix for 1200 s at 150 rpm, then settle for 300 s and measure both phase fractions and phase_ratio by pre-separation HPLC. Its duration×speed equals batch 8’s 300 s×600 rpm while duration resembles batch 12. A result near batch 8’s organic fraction of 0.386 would favor a contact-dose description. A result near batch 12’s 0.473 would favor primarily time-limited equilibration. A much lower result, toward batch 11’s 0.326, would indicate that adequate shear is required and reject simple dose equivalence. An intermediate result would leave time and speed jointly influential; one batch would still not quantify process variance.

3. The final assays were underused in prediction. They supported retention accounting—for example, batches 9 and 11 retained aqueous target close to their pre-separation HPLC values—but their purity and impurity patterns were not incorporated because the requested endpoints were pre-removal target fractions. The observed variation in measured phase_ratio among nominally balanced batches was also simplified when projecting unmeasured recipes.

The least reliable predictions are Q08, Q11, and Q12 because S2–X3 was not tested and their intervals depend on extrapolated interaction and mixing behavior. Q09–Q10 are also fragile because the campaign never changed duration while holding rpm fixed. More generally, every prediction inherits the untested transfer from reagent-containing campaign batches to reagent-omitting queries. Q05 versus Q06 is comparatively better anchored by the direct S0–X0 and S0–X3 screen contrast in batches 1 and 4.

There is a real but disclosed modeling tension between the sealed report and predictions. The report rejected a universal constant-distribution law and emphasized interactions, sparse coverage, and approximate—not exact—mass closure. The predictions nevertheless had to supply points, so they imposed complementary aqueous/organic fractions and transferable empirical adjustments for phase amount and mixing. They also extrapolated an unobserved S2–X3 interaction. Those choices do not alter the sealed report, but they make the prediction intervals model-dependent and arguably too structured relative to the report’s cautions.
